<description>
Split out of #36608, the overall private broadcast rework to support ease of review for like-for-like feature.

Differences from #36608 :
1. No tool support or prep refactors for the tool
2. No package relay
3. Slimmed down test profile focusing on protecting aginst IP address linkage and not crashing the node on adversarial inputs (which is a leak in itself)

With `-privatebroadcast`, `sendrawtransaction` queues a job instead of handing the transaction to
the connection manager. Each job runs on its own thread, shares no state with the node, and
reaches the network only through the Tor proxy: it resolves the chain's DNS seeds, then announces
over BIP324 to recipients on a schedule drawn up front, each connection with fresh isolation
credentials. Nothing a recipient does, and nothing the node sees of the transaction coming back,
changes the plan, and the transaction enters the node's mempool only when it returns from the
network. The old private broadcast connections and relay are removed.

The invariants are specified in `doc/design/private-broadcast.md`.

The rest of the tests are in a follow-up to be considered later:
https://github.com/instagibbs/bitcoin/tree/2026-10-pb_reimpl_followup
</description>

[2026-10-29] c:6488628925 comment by ajtowns (member) (edited 2026-10-29):
[quoted text omitted]

I think what we have is better than nothing, but I believe the argument you're making is that the relevant alternative isn't nothing, but rather people using an independent tool like https://github.com/alfred-hodler/pushtx and that doing so is better than what we have now (because, being independent, it doesn't risk leaks due to node state contamination).

A quick AI analysis suggests that pushtx has its own failings: if tor isn't available it will just drop to clearnet, it gets the peers to connect to via clearnet DNS, and it allows its connections to be correlated to each other by listening for and reacting to the INV for its own transaction. The alternative approach of using tor to connect to a block explorer's push-tx api endpoint works for privacy, but is obviously pretty terrible for censorship resistance. So I think I'm not really convinced that what we have, even with its flaws, isn't better than the actual alternatives. (I think I am convinced that improving those alternatives is a better path than trying to have an in-node solution that's not contaminated by in-node state though)

[quoted text omitted]
I think it's a mistake in both theory and practice for people to assume Core developers are infallible with regard to crypto or privacy concerns. Getting things right is a matter of correcting mistakes when they occur, not never making mistakes. Trying to satisfy people who expect us never to make mistakes isn't going to work -- the best we can possibly do is satisfy people who expect that we'll tell them when we make mistakes and that we'll do our best to fix those mistakes.

I think you might want to review #35858 as the recommendations there seem stronger than is justified ("The transaction reaches the wider network only once a recipient relays it, which prevents linking the submission to the node's IP address.")

In any event, it sounds to me like a better approach to this feature would be:

 * abandon the approach of in-node support for private broadcast -- there's too much risk of state contamination that defeats the entire purpose of the feature for realistic adversarial scenarios
 * deprecate the existing feature in point updates to existing releases -- what we have isn't something we can really recommend that people use (change it to `-privatebroadcast=allow-deprecated` to continue enabling it perhaps)
 * provide a BIP/spec for private broadcast behaviour, with discussion of the tradeoffs and risks. if different people strongly prefer different approaches, have multiple BIPs as appropriate
 * provide external tools implementing the approach documented in the spec(s)
 * add a hook so that `sendrawtransaction` always uses a specified external tool
 * add a hook so that wallet broadcast (and wallet rebroadcast) always uses a specified external tool rather than adding to the mempool or relaying directly (goal here would be to reduce linkage between txs in different wallets, I think)
 * include an in-repo implementation of a spec whose tradeoffs are reasonable/broadly acceptable and bundle it with bitcoind

I don't have a strong preference as to order; but deprecating the feature shouldn't be delayed pending other steps if our feature either is not something we can recommend as fit for purpose and/or is worse than using alternative third party tools.

(Even in this scenario, there's a potential linkage between node and tx: the wallet will likely only rebroadcast once the tx in question exits your mempool)

Apart from "include an in-repo implementation of a spec" I think all of those should be relatively small or negative-LOC PRs as far as the bitcoin core repo is concerned, so relatively easy to review.

(To clarify maybe: this is my opinion on an approach would most easily meet everyone's goals here; it's not meant to be an ultimatum, or a "your ideas are bad and should be thrown away" against anyone)
[2026-10-29] c:6489688006 comment by ajtowns (member):
[quoted text omitted]

I think an extreme attack scenario worth thinking about here is:

 * about 50% of the reachable addresses in your addrman that also function as a working node (ie, will give you a good headers chain, respond to pings etc) are honest nodes. this is sufficient for addrman's goal of "preventing a single entity from occupying all outbound slots" with 99% chance
 * the remaining 50% of reachable addresses in your addrman (or more, given the additional constraints above) are attacker controlled
 * not only that, most of them (say 42% of addrman entries) are roughly unique to your node -- they were given to only you by the attacker, and you didn't successfully relay them to an honest outbound, because addr relay is probabilistic not flood fill).
 * when you make three outbound connections to do private broadcast, you have ~80% chance of one of those connections being to an attacker controlled address that has not been shared with anyone else, linking that transaction with your node (because the attacker only gave that address to your node), and hence with your other transactions

Hopefully that exact attack is unrealistic, given the expectation that the attacker has to provide perhaps ~650M unique addresses in total (18k addresses for each of 18k public nodes to be 50% of reachable addresses, but unique for each node?) all with a reachable bitcoin node answering them, ready to spy on relayed transactions. It's meant to be a thought-experiment, not an attack recipe, after all.

In that scenario, addrman, block relay and transaction relay all continue to work as specced and the node is not eclipsed, because you do have at least one honest outbound connection, but a pervasive group attempting to do tx linking still immediately succeeds in identifying 4-out-of-5 private broadcast txs.

[quoted text omitted]
I don't think you can reasonably say "this is an experimental feature" and "it should be default and enabled by node-in-a-box implementations" at the same time.

But also, shipping a privacy branded feature with known architectural defects which permit breaching the promised privacy under a very reasonable threat model, is worse than shipping nothing.

[quoted text omitted]
However for that part, no, this is not the argument i was making. What i had in mind was simply broadcasting the transaction through Tor to one of the many available broadcast API out there. A simple `curl` using your Tor proxy is sufficient here, and i know of multiple people who have been doing just that in the past. Some popular explorers like Mempool's or Blockstream's offer hidden services and even a webpage for transaction submission ([1](http://mempoolhqx4isw62xs7abwphsq7ldayuidyx2v2oethdhhj6mlo2r6ad.onion/tx/push), [2](http://explorerzydxu5ecjrkwceayqybizmjjznk5izmitf2modhcusuqlid.onion/tx/push)), so less technical users can use the Tor browser instead of the command line.

It is indeed less reliable as it's limited to a few single points of failures, and if we can offer a more decentralized option i'm all in, but i don't think this should compromise on privacy, which is the desired property in the first place.

That said i am skeptical we could realistically achieve this. I think that would merely shift the single point of failures from explorer APIs towards DNS seeds, and while there may be reasons why the latter may be reasonable, that does not seem like a particularly interesting goal.

Instead, the value i see in private broadcast is to make this limited tool, which allows one to trade-off reliability for substantially improved privacy, available to more people. If we can implement it properly, i think it could have some pretty interesting properties at scale: some turnkey node solutions could start defaulting to using it by default for broadcasting the transactions from wallet commonly associated with these boxes, and if a few % of transactions on the network start being broadcast this way it might create enough false positives to defeat spies' transaction origin analysis.

This perspective is why i'm supporting this attempt to salvage the feature rather than stripping it off entirely.
